title: Senate Commerce punts AI legislation to September, advances kids online safety package
subtitle: Chair Ted Cruz postponed a highly anticipated markup on frontier-AI bills after bipartisan talks stalled, sending the CHATBOT Act and the Youth AI Privacy Act into September while KOSA moves ahead.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee on July 30 postponed action on its broader AI legislative package until after the August recess, delaying a markup that lawmakers had spent most of July trying to lock down. Committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) proceeded with an August 5 vote on the Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA, S.1748) and related child-safety bills — the SCREEN Act, the Youth AI Privacy Act, the CHATBOT Act, and the Children's Artificial Intelligence Toy Safety Act — but the frontier-AI items members had been arguing over, including a state-preemption framework and pre-release model review, will slip to September.

The reason the AI package stalled matters more than the delay itself. Republican and Democratic staff have been unable to close a gap on whether federal AI rules should preempt the growing patchwork of state laws — California, Colorado, Illinois, Texas, and New York all now have binding AI statutes on the books — and on how much authority the executive branch should have over frontier-model releases. Industry has pushed hard for preemption because the compliance cost of running separate programs in each state is now measurable, while advocacy groups have pushed back that preemption without a strong federal floor would trade real state protections for weaker federal ones.

This lands into a week where the Trump administration was reported to be finalizing a voluntary 30-day national-security review framework with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google — a parallel executive-branch track that would establish some frontier-model oversight without waiting for Congress. The interaction between the two is the substantive question. If the voluntary framework holds and the labs cooperate, the pressure to pass anything binding drops, and September markup slips again. If a public incident forces the issue, the negotiated language that got tabled this week may be what Congress reaches for first.

For learners: US AI regulation is being written in three places at once — Congress, the executive branch, and state capitals — and the interactions between them are more important than any single vote. When a Senate committee delays a markup, watch what happens in the parallel executive negotiation and in the state legislatures over the same period. The binding rules that will actually apply to AI systems in 2027 will come from whichever of those three tracks moves fastest, and this week the answer is neither Congress nor the states.
